summary: Documents an already deployed RADIUS extension in which a client can query whether a RADIUS server is working, using the Status-Server packet code that RFC 2865 reserved for experimental use. It is informational and not an Internet standard.

eli5.summary: A network gate keeper sometimes wants to know if the person who checks passwords is still at their desk. This describes a simple "are you there?" message for RADIUS servers.

questions: how to check if a radius server is alive
why not use access-request to test radius
does status-server get forwarded by proxies
subtitle: A RADIUS packet that asks a server whether it is alive without pretending to be a user login.

tldr.problem: A RADIUS client that gets no reply cannot tell whether the server is down. Probing with Access-Request or Accounting-Request looks like a real login or accounting event, with unwanted side effects.
tldr.mechanism: The client sends a Status-Server packet (Code 12) containing a mandatory Message-Authenticator. The server answers with an Access-Accept on the authentication port or an Accounting-Response on the accounting port, and proxies never forward the packet.
tldr.outcome: It gives a hop-by-hop liveness check that supports failover. It is an Informational description of a deployed extension rather than a standard, and it cannot tell whether a specific realm is reachable.

today: RFC 5997 is an Informational RFC that updates RFC 2865. Its metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What Status-Server Is
sections.content:
This RFC specifies a deployed extension to RADIUS that lets a client query the status of a server. RFC 2865 defined the Status-Server Code (12) as experimental but gave no details of its operation. Like core RADIUS, the extension is stateless, and queries have no side effects other than perhaps incrementing a packet counter. The document covers only UDP transport.

It is Informational rather than Standards Track because of problems with deployed implementations, including security vulnerabilities. Some implementations do not support the Message-Authenticator attribute, which lets an unauthorized client spoof Status-Server packets, so this specification requires it.
sections.eli5: RADIUS servers check passwords for networks. Status-Server is a polite way for the network gear to ask 'are you still working?'

sections.title: Why Not Just Use Access-Request
sections.content:
A status check sent as an Access-Request or Accounting-Request can be mistaken for a real user. The server may think a user logged on, send an Access-Challenge or Access-Reject, warn an administrator about failed logins, or delay a reject as rate limiting, leaving the sender unsure whether the server is down or just slow. Test users created for this purpose could be abused by an attacker. Accounting-Request needs mandatory attributes, so fake values must be supplied and may pollute the accounting database.

NAS implementors SHOULD NOT generate Access-Request or Accounting-Request packets solely to see if a server is alive, and administrators SHOULD NOT configure test users solely for that purpose. Status-Server is also not the 'Keep-Alive' mentioned in RFC 2865.
sections.eli5: If you pretend to be a customer just to see if a shop is open, the staff might start serving you. A plain 'are you open?' avoids the mix-up.

sections.title: The Status-Server Packet
sections.content:
Status-Server reuses the RADIUS packet format from RFC 2865. The Request Authenticator is a 16-octet random number that SHOULD be unpredictable and unique over the lifetime of the shared secret. Every packet MUST include a Message-Authenticator attribute, otherwise it could be trivially spoofed. It MAY include NAS-Identifier and one of NAS-IP-Address or NAS-IPv6-Address, and other attributes SHOULD NOT be included. User credentials such as User-Name and User-Password MUST NOT appear in packets to an authentication port, and accounting attributes MUST NOT appear in packets to an accounting port.

The server replies with an Access-Accept (authentication port) or an Accounting-Response (accounting port) and MUST NOT send more than one response. The Response Authenticator is computed as MD5(Code+ID+Length+RequestAuth+Attributes+Secret). The same request definition is used for both ports, so only the response varies by port.
sections.eli5: The knock has a secret handshake so nobody can fake it, and the answer is a short stamped reply with no extra chatter.

sections.title: Client and Server Behavior
sections.content:
Clients SHOULD let administrators enable or disable Status-Server globally and per server, with the default disabled. They SHOULD use a watchdog timer as in RFC 5080. A Status-Server packet MUST NOT be retransmitted; instead a new packet is sent with a new Identifier and Authenticator. Clients may use the same source port as normal requests (the Identifier must then be unique across outstanding requests) or a unique port. They should accept any validly signed Access-Accept or Accounting-Response as the reply.

Servers SHOULD allow enabling or disabling acceptance, with the default enabled. They MUST silently discard packets from unknown clients or with a bad Message-Authenticator, SHOULD discard packets from clients sending too many, and MAY stay silent if they cannot do their normal work, for example when a database is down.

Proxies MUST NOT forward Status-Server, so the answer reports on that one server only. If a client gets no reply, it can fail over to another server and keep probing the first to learn when it recovers.
sections.eli5: The asker never repeats the same question; it asks a fresh one each time. The answerer can ignore people who ask too often.

sections.title: Limits and Security
sections.content:
Status-Server cannot tell whether a particular realm is reachable. Because servers reply without examining User-Name, a proxy that is up but cannot reach one realm still looks responsive. The RFC says a robust fix would need a routing table or a 'destination unreachable' response, which are outside its scope, and recommends combining Status-Server with server failover.

Early implementations that did not enforce Message-Authenticator allowed a reflected DoS attack on a real client. They also allowed a race in which an attacker copied the Request Authenticator from a valid Access-Request, and the server could answer with an Access-Accept and authorize unwanted service. Implementations that do not require Message-Authenticator are NOT RECOMMENDED. The RFC also notes that RADIUS relies on MD5, and that IETF efforts to address its weakness were ongoing.
sections.eli5: The 'are you home?' check only says the front desk is awake. It cannot say whether the back office behind it is working.
